summary:
Sliding window with the last index of each character. Move the right edge one step at a time; if the new
character was last seen inside the window, the window can't contain both copies, so jump the left edge to just
after that last position. The window is always fresh; track its largest length. O(n).

question.md:
Return the length of the longest substring of `s` with no repeated character.

- **n up to 10⁵**, letters and digits (36 possible characters).

**Edge cases to keep in mind**

- A single character: the answer is 1.
- All characters different: the whole string.
- A repeat **outside** the current window (like the first `a` in `abba` when we reach the last `a`) must not
  move the window.

think.md:
**The rule and its shape.** A window is valid when no character appears twice in it. Shrinking a valid window
keeps it valid, and growing an invalid one keeps it invalid. That's the signature of a "longest valid window"
problem.

**Why the left edge never goes back.** If the window `[L, R]` breaks the rule, then every longer window `[L, R']` with
`R' > R` contains it and breaks the rule too. So once a start `L` fails for some `R`, it fails for all later `R`, and
we can throw it away forever. That's what lets the left pointer only move forward, and makes the whole scan O(n).
**A trace on `"abcabdcbb"`.** `R` adds one character per row; `L` is moved just far enough to remove the repeat:

**Moving `L` faster.** When the new character `c` repeats inside the window, the window must start **after the
previous `c`**: any start at or before it still contains both copies. Instead of stepping `L` one character at a
time, remember the last index of each character and jump straight there.

**The stale-entry trap.** The remembered index may already be left of `L` (the earlier copy was dropped long
ago). Then nothing repeats inside the window, and `L` must not move. In `"abba"`, at the final `a` the last `a`
is at 0 but `L` is already 2; jumping to 1 would move `L` backwards and allow `"bba"`, which isn't fresh. So the
jump is taken only if `last[c] ≥ L`.

idea.md:
For each start `i`, walk right adding characters to a "seen" set until the next character is already
seen. The run `s[i..j−1]` is the longest fresh run starting at `i`.

Because there are only 36 possible characters, a fresh run is at most 36 long, so each start stops
quickly here. But with a large alphabet (say all Unicode) this becomes O(n²), and it re-reads the same
characters from many starts.

lines.text: The longest fresh run found so far.

Each position as the start of a run. Every index is tried as the left end of the window. Nothing learned from one start is reused for the next, which is exactly the waste the better approaches remove.
Grow the run while the next character hasn't appeared in it yet. The "seen" set (or array) is rebuilt for every start.
The run from this start is `j − i` long; keep the longest.

complexity.md: **Time O(n · σ)**, where σ is the number of distinct characters (36 here, up to n in general). **Space O(σ)** for the seen set.

steps.text: Start 0: the window grows to 0..2 (length 3). Adding a at 3 would break the rule, so this start stops.
Start 1: the window grows to 1..3 (length 3). Adding b at 4 would break the rule, so this start stops.
Start 2: the window grows to 2..5 (length 4). Adding c at 6 would break the rule, so this start stops.
Start 3: the window grows to 3..6 (length 4). Adding b at 7 would break the rule, so this start stops.
Start 4: the window grows to 4..6 (length 3). Adding b at 7 would break the rule, so this start stops.
Start 5: the window grows to 5..7 (length 3). Adding b at 8 would break the rule, so this start stops.
Starts 6..8 are checked the same way. The longest window starts at 2. In total about 33 cells were re-read, which grows like n²: the same cells are scanned again from every start.

walk.title: From each start, extend until a character repeats.

limits.md: With a small alphabet each start stops within 37 characters, but with a large one (or unrestricted text) this is O(n²), and characters are rescanned from every start. Remembering where each character was last seen lets the window jump past a repeat directly.

approaches.title: Sliding window with last positions

idea.md:
One pass with `R` over the string, and `L` as the start of the current fresh window. `last[c]` stores the
most recent index of character `c`.

For each `R` with character `c`:

1. If `last[c] ≥ L`, the previous `c` is inside the window; set `L = last[c] + 1`.
2. Record `last[c] = R`.
3. The window `s[L..R]` is fresh; update the best length with `R − L + 1`.

**Invariant.** After step 1, `s[L..R]` has no repeated character, and `L` is the smallest start for which
that's true. Since every fresh window ending at `R` starts at `L` or later, `R − L + 1` is the longest
one ending at `R`; taking the max over all `R` gives the answer.

build: `last` maps each character to its latest index (or −1); `L = 0`, `best = 0`.
For each `R`: if `last[s[R]] ≥ L`, jump `L` to `last[s[R]] + 1`.

lines.text: `last[c]` is the latest index of character `c` (−1 = never seen). `L` is where the current fresh window starts.

notes.java: An array indexed by character code beats a map.
notes.cpp: An array indexed by character code beats a map.
notes.c: An array indexed by character code.

lines.text: Take the character at `R` into the window and record that it was seen here.

If this character's previous copy lies **inside** the window (`last[c] ≥ L`), the window must start just after it. If the previous copy is already left of `L`, it's irrelevant, and moving `L` would wrongly move it backwards.
After the repair, `L … R` is the longest valid window that ends at `R` (no earlier start works). Comparing its length with the best covers every possible right end.

complexity.md:
**Time O(n):** one step per character; `L` jumps in O(1). **Space O(σ)** for `last` (a 128-entry
array in Java, C++ and C).

steps.text: 'a' at 3 was last seen inside the window, so left jumps to 1. Window 'bca'.
'b' at 4 was last seen inside the window, so left jumps to 2. Window 'cab'.
'c' at 6 was last seen inside the window, so left jumps to 3. Window 'abdc'.
'b' at 7 was last seen inside the window, so left jumps to 5. Window 'dcb'.
'b' at 8 was last seen inside the window, so left jumps to 8. Window 'b'.

walk.title: Grow the window to the right. When the new character already sits inside the window, jump the left edge just past its previous position.

takeaways.md:
- **Longest window with "no repeats"** → sliding window with last-seen positions.
- **Jump, don't crawl:** `L = last[c] + 1`, but only if `last[c] ≥ L` (ignore stale positions).
- **Template for longest-valid-window:** for each `R`: add, fix the window by moving `L`, record `R − L + 1`.
